# From Plateaus to Paradigms

**A History of AI and Our Future** — a Slidev deck for a technical lecture hosted by the
Fudan University supercomputing team, September 2026.

A companion piece to [Theory of Computation](https://github.com/AIxMath/Lecture-TOC):
same Slidev + seriph toolchain, same `routerMode: hash` deployment, denser layout.

**88 slides. 24 figures generated, 22 used, every one generated by a script in this repo.**
Most are computed rather than drawn — gradient descent is actually run, the bias–variance curve is
an actual experiment, the Hopfield panel is an actual network settling, the roofline uses real H100 specs.
Every slide carries presenter notes in Chinese — the speaker presents in Chinese, the slides are English.

## Running it

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev        # http://localhost:3030
pnpm build      # static build into dist/
pnpm export     # render to PDF/PNG (needs playwright-chromium)
```

Deploys as-is to Vercel (`vercel.json`) or Netlify (`netlify.toml`).

## The argument

1. **Act I** — the five paradigms (symbolic/expert systems → backpropagation → statistical
   learning → deep learning → transformers and scale), each following the same arc: an idea,
   a rush, a slowdown in structural progress, a long refinement phase, and then the next idea,
   built from what the refinement produced. The mechanisms that survive live here too, next to
   the paradigm they belong to, so the timeline is walked once rather than twice: Hopfield and
   the perceptron sit inside the connectionist paradigm, attention and the scaling laws inside
   the transformer paradigm. Backpropagation, gradient descent, convolution, recurrence and the
   representation-learning slides were cut — the connectionist paradigm now runs idea → what it
   built → where it stopped, and the mechanism detail belongs to a later lecture.
2. **Act II** — the present. Three years of IMO results, the 2026 AI-for-mathematics wave
   (Erdős, Fermat), the credit disputes, and two evaluators disagreeing about the same model
   by a hundred points — which is the evidence thread, told through results rather than
   through a slide about evidence standards.
3. **Act III** — the honest ledger, the costs, what the education RCTs actually found, and
   four dispositions worth having. The three AI-for-science slides were cut; the speaker covers
   that ground verbally, and the ledger table stays as the visual anchor for it.

## Figures

All are produced by `scripts/make_charts.py` from two datasets plus one curated price
table. Nothing is hand-drawn, and every number on a chart is computed at build time.

**Every figure is emitted twice — a light and a dark variant.** The deck is presented in
dark mode, where the light variant's dark ink would be invisible. `components/Chart.vue`
renders both and `style.css` shows whichever matches the current scheme, so a slide writes
`<Chart name="compute-vs-moore" width="790px" />` once and works in either theme. The
palette is contrast-checked on every build: the script prints the WCAG ratio of each text
colour against its own slide background, and fails loudly in review if a colour drops below
AA. Data scatter uses a deliberately recessive colour, which is marked as such.

| Figure | What it shows | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compute-vs-moore.svg` | Notable-model training compute 1950–2026, fitted trend vs a Moore's-law line. Measured doubling: **2× / 5.6 months**, against Moore's 2× / 24 months — a ~10⁷× gap by 2026. | Epoch notable-models, 538 models with disclosed compute |
| `params-capability.svg` | Two panels: model size over time (and the post-2024 disclosure cliff), and GPQA Diamond capability over time. | Epoch notable-models + Epoch benchmark runs (311 GPQA runs) |
| `benchmark-saturation.svg` | Three benchmarks saturating in turn, from real runs rather than vendor claims. | Epoch runs: GPQA, OTIS Mock AIME, FrontierMath Tier 4 |
| `chinchilla-shift.svg` | Parameters vs training tokens, with the 20:1 Chinchilla line. Measured median tokens-per-parameter: **1.1 before 2022 → 21.5 after**. | Epoch notable-models, 458 models with both |
| `price-performance.svg` | Measured intelligence against list price for all **145** comparable models, with the efficiency frontier drawn in. Shows the cheap tier collapsing and the top of the frontier costing 92× more for 11 further points; 6 of the 9 frontier models are open-weight. | Artificial Analysis leaderboard, 652 models captured, filtered to the 170 ranked under the current index version |
| `energy-queue.svg` | Global datacenter electricity, and the gap between grid capacity requested and capacity actually energized (~3%). | IEA 2026 update; ERCOT queue |
| `claimed-vs-audited.svg` | The announced number against the number that survives an independent test, across three domains. | A-Lab audit, SWE-bench Pro, FeatureBench |
| `harness-effect.svg` | One model, two *verified* scores, and the 37-point gap between harnesses. Deliberately framed as harness sensitivity, not as a failed claim. | ARC Prize verified results, GPT-6 Astra on ARC-AGI-3 |
| `paradigm-timeline.svg` | The five paradigms with each one's internal arc. Explicitly labelled as an interpretive reading, not a measurement. | Interpretation; dates from the historical record |
| `paradigm-cycle.svg` | One curve per paradigm showing fast structural gains then diminishing returns, with the envelope resetting at each transition. Vertical axis labelled illustrative, not measured. | Interpretation |
| `imagenet-error.svg` | ILSVRC top-5 error 2010–2017 against both human baselines. Every point is the official competition test-set result, with ensembles flagged. | image-net.org official results pages, cross-checked against the winning papers |
| `xor.svg` | XOR is not linearly separable, and one hidden layer fixes it. The boundary, and the two hidden-unit band, are both computed. | Computed |
| `learning-rate.svg` | Real gradient descent on a non-convex loss at three step sizes: too slow, converges, and overshoots clear out of the frame. | Simulated |
| `bias-variance.svg` | Polynomials of increasing degree fitted to noisy samples, 240 draws, median training and test error. Best degree 3; degree 12 is 140× worse. | Simulated |
| `scaling-shapes.svg` | The three scaling axes in their real functional forms — a power law, a sigmoid, and a saturating curve. Only one is a straight line on a log axis. | Functional forms |
| `roofline.svg` | The roofline for one H100 (989 TFLOP/s dense BF16, 3.35 TB/s HBM; ridge at 295 FLOP/byte), with matmul, attention and single-token decoding placed on it. | Published H100 specs; intensities computed from op shapes |
| `hopfield.svg` | A real 100-neuron Hopfield network storing five patterns, started from four corruption levels. Energy never rises; the corrupted states fall into memory. | Simulated |
| `attention-paths.svg` | Recurrent distance O(n) against self-attention O(1). A schematic, and labelled as one. | Schematic |
| `education-rct.svg` | Bastani et al.: the same model with two tutor designs — +48%/+127% on practice, but −17%/0% on the exam taken without AI. | Published effect sizes |
| `metr-productivity.svg` | METR's randomised trial: developers forecast +24%, were measured at −19%, and believed +20% afterwards. | Published study |

Rebuild them after editing the script:

```bash
python3 scripts/make_charts.py     # needs pandas, numpy, matplotlib
```

Data inputs live in `research/`: `research/scratch/epoch.csv` (Epoch AI notable models) and
`research/data/benchmarks.csv` (Epoch AI benchmark runs).

## Layout

The canvas is 980×552. Three rules in `style.css` keep every slide occupying its frame:

1. **Vertical balance.** The title stays pinned to the top and the remaining content centres
   itself in whatever height is left, so a short slide reads as deliberate rather than
   unfinished. Done with an auto margin on `h1 + *` and on `*:last-child`, which split the
   free space; a slide that already fills has no free space and does not move.
   Before this, the median slide carried ~200px of dead space stacked at the bottom and 29
   slides had more than 230px of it.

2. **Table spacing, not table stretching.** An intermediate version let a table absorb all the
   leftover height. It filled the frame, but the row height then depended on the row count: a
   four-row table ended up with 106px rows and a seven-row table with 65px ones, which reads as
   padded rather than designed. The table now keeps its natural height with comfortable row
   padding (34px rows, one type size for the whole deck) and the block is centred. A short
   table on a short slide is then a deliberately airy slide, which is what a thirty-second list
   slide should look like.

3. **Figure centring.** The figure wrapper is narrower than the text column, so it is centred
   with CSS margins rather than an inline `margin: 0 auto` — an inline shorthand would also
   zero the vertical auto margins rule 1 depends on, which silently disabled the balance on
   every chart slide until it was caught.

## Verification

Slidev silently clips content that overflows the 980×552 canvas, and chart labels can
collide in ways that are invisible until you present. `scripts/verify.mjs` measures both by
driving a headless browser:

```bash
node scripts/verify.mjs            # build, serve, check everything
node scripts/verify.mjs --no-build # reuse dist/
```

It reports, for every slide, whether anything reaches the bottom edge, and for every chart,
whether any two text labels overlap or fall outside the frame. It runs the slide pass
**twice, in light and dark mode**, and asserts that the *correct* figure variant is visible
in each — not merely that one of them is. It also fails on any slide carrying two adjacent
HTML comments, since Slidev silently keeps only the last one as the presenter note, and on a
`---` that got glued to the end of the previous line, which is not a fence and merges two
slides into one while leaving the count plausible.

Text-on-text collisions are checked separately from chart labels, per **line** rather than
per element. The seriph theme hard-codes several line-heights in rem —
`.slidev-layout p { line-height: 1.5rem }`, `[text-4xl=""] { line-height: 2.5rem }` — so a
60px font can sit in a 24px line box and paint 79px outside it. The element boxes do not
overlap; only the glyphs do, which is why "the g in Prologue collides with 1969" is the kind
of thing that survives a geometric check. `getClientRects()` is required here, not
`getBoundingClientRect()`: an `<em>` spanning a line break has one bounding box covering both
lines and would report a collision with everything on them.

Current state: **88/88 slides fit in both modes, 48/48 chart files clean, no text overlaps, one
note per slide.**

Two figures are generated but no longer placed: `learning-rate` and `scaling-shapes`, from the
gradient-descent and three-scaling-axes slides. Those slides were cut, and the figures are kept
in `public/charts/` in case they are wanted back. Chart labels are measured with `getBoundingClientRect`, not
`getBBox` — matplotlib puts each label in its own `<g transform>`, so `getBBox` returns
pre-transform coordinates and cross-label comparisons against it are meaningless.

## Sourcing

Every non-obvious number is traceable to a primary source. The working notes are in
`research/briefings/`, including `ai-history-factcheck-1943-2026.md`, which checked 42
historical claims and corrected several that are commonly repeated but wrong:

- Simon & Newell's chess prediction is **1958**, not 1965; the "twenty years" line is Simon 1960.
- "Artificial intelligence" appears in the **1955 Dartmouth proposal**, not at the 1956 workshop.
- AlexNet's 15.3% and ResNet's 3.57% are **ensemble** results (single models: 18.2% and 4.49%).
- ImageNet's 14M images / 20k categories is the **2014** release; the 2009 paper launched with 3.2M.
- XCON's "$40M a year" is not primary-sourced; the documented figure is roughly **$25M a year**.
- LSTM had no forget gate until **2000**.
- The LISP-machine decline was gradual (**1987–1993**), not a clean 1987 collapse.
- The 2026 perfect IMO score is a **company announcement via state media**, not an IMO-published result.

Charts carry their own caveats on the slide where the data is thinner than it looks: the
price chart notes that per-token price understates reasoning-model cost, the saturation
chart notes that FrontierMath is graded by automated answer-checking rather than verified
proofs, and the timeline is labelled as interpretation.

### A correction worth keeping

An earlier draft put ARC-AGI-3's two numbers (62.7% and 99.9%) into the "claimed versus
audited" figure, which implied the higher one was not a real result. That was wrong. ARC
Prize publishes **both** as verified scores on the same results page, because they answer
two different questions — a neutral cross-provider interface versus the provider's own
context management — and states it will report both going forward, each clearly labelled.
The case now has its own figure framed as harness sensitivity, and the audit figure is down
to the three domains where a claim genuinely failed an independent test. The rule applied
here: a result that a benchmark's own maintainers publish and explain is not a marketing
number, however convenient that would be for the argument.
